title: Writing: An Opinion Essay on Media Responsibility

writingModel.placeholder: State the issue and your position — use a that-clause or wh-clause for precision
writingModel.hint: e.g. "It is clear that…" / "What matters is…" / "The question of whether… is central."

writingModel.placeholder: First argument with evidence — use noun clauses to report research or state facts
writingModel.hint: "Research has shown that…" / "It has been established that…" / "The fact that… is significant."

writingModel.placeholder: Second argument or counter-argument — use embedded questions to frame the debate
writingModel.hint: "The question of whether… remains contested." / "Critics wonder whether…"

writingModel.placeholder: Third argument — use emphasis structures combined with noun clauses
writingModel.hint: "What the evidence makes clear is that…" / "It is not… but… that is the problem."

writingModel.placeholder: Conclusion — use a noun clause to frame the key takeaway
writingModel.hint: "What is needed is…" / "It is essential that…" / "The question is not whether… but how…"

writingTemplate.suffix: poses a significant threat to democratic society.
writingTemplate.placeholder: the rise of disinformation / the decline of independent local journalism
writingTemplate.hint: "It is clear that + clause" — noun clause as the real subject

writingTemplate.placeholder: emotional content spreads far faster than corrections / news deserts correlate with higher local corruption
writingTemplate.hint: "Research has shown that + clause" — reporting verb + that-clause

writingTemplate.suffix: is one of the most contested issues in media policy today.
writingTemplate.placeholder: social media platforms should be regulated as publishers / AI-generated content should be labelled
writingTemplate.hint: "The question of whether + S + V" — noun phrase + embedded question

writingTemplate.prefix: What the evidence makes clear is that
writingTemplate.placeholder: media literacy education must be treated as a priority equal to science or mathematics
writingTemplate.hint: "What + S + V + is that + clause" — wh-cleft for emphasis

writingTemplate.prefix: The question is not whether we should act, but
writingTemplate.placeholder: how quickly and decisively we choose to do so
writingTemplate.hint: "The question is not whether… but how/what/when…" — embedded questions for conclusion

items: It is clear that the media landscape has changed fundamentally.
What concerns many researchers is the speed at which false information spreads.
The fact that 100 companies control most of the world's media is deeply significant.
Whether social media companies bear responsibility for the content they host is a growing legal question.
That misinformation can influence elections is now well documented.
Research has demonstrated that emotional content is shared more widely than factual reporting.
It has been established that news deserts correlate with higher local corruption.
Studies have found that corrections reach far fewer people than the original false claims.
It is widely accepted that filter bubbles can reinforce existing beliefs.
The evidence suggests that media literacy programmes can significantly reduce susceptibility to disinformation.
The question of whether platforms should be treated as publishers remains unresolved.
Researchers are examining whether media literacy education is sufficient on its own.
The matter of who funds journalism significantly affects what gets reported.
It is unclear how quickly AI-generated deepfakes will undermine trust in visual media.
Critics wonder whether self-regulation by large platforms can ever be adequate.
What is needed is a combination of regulation, education, and civic engagement.
It is essential that citizens develop critical skills for evaluating information.
The question is not whether action is needed, but how urgently it must be taken.
What the evidence ultimately suggests is that a healthy media environment requires active support.
Whether we choose to act on this knowledge is, ultimately, a question of democratic will.

questions.text: "It is clear ___ media ownership affects the content and framing of news." (noun clause)
questions.hint: "It is clear that + clause" — standard noun clause after evaluative expression

questions.text: "Research has demonstrated ___ emotional content spreads significantly faster than corrections."
"The question of ___ social media platforms should be regulated as publishers is highly contested."
questions.hint: "The question of whether + S + V" — embedded yes/no question after preposition

questions.text: "___ the evidence makes clear is that media literacy must become a core educational priority." (wh-cleft + that-clause)
questions.hint: "What + S + V + is that + clause" — combined wh-cleft + that-clause

questions.text: "The question is not ___ we should act, but ___ urgently we choose to do so."
questions.hint: "Not whether… but how…" — two embedded questions for contrast

questions.text: "The debate about if self-regulation is adequate" is correct formal English.
questions.hint: After prepositions: only "whether" — "the debate about whether"

questions.text: "___ matters is not just what we read but ___ we evaluate what we read." (two wh-clauses)
questions.hint: "What + S + V + is + noun clause" — what matters is how we evaluate

questions.text: "It is essential ___ journalism is funded independently of commercial and political interests."
questions.hint: "It is essential that + clause" — formal recommendation + noun clause
